records.source: וְ֠נַעֲמָן שַׂר־צְבָ֨א מֶֽלֶךְ־אֲרָ֜ם הָיָ֣ה אִישׁ֩ גָּד֨וֹל לִפְנֵ֤י אֲדֹנָיו֙ וּנְשֻׂ֣א פָנִ֔ים כִּֽי־ב֛וֹ נָֽתַן־יְהוָ֥ה תְּשׁוּעָ֖ה לַאֲרָ֑ם וְהָאִ֗ישׁ הָיָ֛ה גִּבּ֥וֹר חַ֖יִל מְצֹרָֽע׃
records.gloss: And Naaman, commander of [the] army of [the] king of Aram, was a man great before his master and lifted up of face, for by him had given Yahweh victory to Aram; and the man was a mighty man of valor, having scale disease.
pieces: Naaman was commander of the army of the king of Aram. His master regarded him as a great man and held him in high honor, because through him {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} had given victory to Aram. He was a mighty warrior, but he had a serious skin disease.

L.1: Now Naaman, commander of the army of the king of Aram, was a great man before his master and lifted up of face, for by him {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} had given victory to Aram. And the man was a mighty man of valor, with scale disease.

R.1: Naaman was the army commander for the king of Aram. His master thought very highly of him and honored him, because {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} had used Naaman to give Aram victory. Naaman was a strong and brave soldier, but he had a serious skin disease.

decisions.choice: scale disease: a serious skin condition that made a person unclean, not modern leprosy
decisions.reason: The word is the one used for the skin diseases of Leviticus 13-14, which are known by visible signs such as raw or flaking patches and hair turning white (Leviticus 13:2-44). Leprosy as known today (Hansen's disease) does not fit those signs well, and the same word is used of a growth in cloth and in house walls (Leviticus 13:47; 14:34). Naaman still serves at court and goes into a temple with his king (verse 18), so Aram did not keep him apart as Israel's law required (Leviticus 13:45-46).

decisions.choice: lifted up of face: held in high honor
decisions.reason: To "lift up someone's face" is to receive him with favor and respect (Genesis 32:21; Job 42:8-9). Naaman stands high in his king's favor, and the next words give the reason.

decisions.choice: Yahweh had given victory to Aram through Naaman
alternatives: the gods of Aram had given the victory
decisions.reason: The writer says that Aram's successes came from Yahweh, the God of Israel, even though Aram did not worship him. Yahweh rules over the nations around Israel too (1 Kings 19:15). The story will end with this foreign commander confessing Yahweh as the only God (verse 15).

decisions.choice: Aram: the kingdom north-east of Israel, with Damascus as its capital
decisions.reason: Aram (Syria) and Israel were often at war in these years (1 Kings 20; 22; 2 Kings 6:8-7:20). The king is not named here; Damascus is its capital (verse 12).

decisions.choice: scale disease (Literal); serious skin disease (Balanced, Readable); mighty man of valor (Literal), mighty warrior (Balanced), strong and brave soldier (Readable)
decisions.reason: The disease is named as in Leviticus 13, so the reader can see that it is the same condition the law describes. Balanced and Readable add "but" to show the contrast the Hebrew makes by setting the disease last.

records.heading: Naaman is healed

records.source: וַאֲרָם֙ יָצְא֣וּ גְדוּדִ֔ים וַיִּשְׁבּ֛וּ מֵאֶ֥רֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל נַעֲרָ֣ה קְטַנָּ֑ה וַתְּהִ֕י לִפְנֵ֖י אֵ֥שֶׁת נַעֲמָֽן׃
records.gloss: And Aram had gone out [in] raiding bands and had taken captive from [the] land of Israel a girl young, and she was before [the] wife of Naaman.
pieces: Raiding parties from Aram had gone out and had taken a young girl captive from the land of Israel, and she served Naaman's wife.

L.2: And Aram had gone out [in] raiding bands and had taken captive from the land of Israel a young girl, and she was before the wife of Naaman.

R.2: Some time before, soldiers from Aram had gone on raids into the land of Israel. They had captured a young girl, and she became a servant to Naaman's wife.

decisions.choice: raiding bands: small armed groups that crossed the border to plunder and take captives
decisions.reason: Raids like these went on even when there was no full war between the kingdoms (6:23; 13:20-21). Captives were taken back to serve in their captors' households.

decisions.choice: she was before Naaman's wife: she served her as an attendant
decisions.reason: To be or stand "before" someone is to wait on that person (1 Kings 1:2; 10:8). The girl, taken from her home, became a servant in the commander's household.

decisions.choice: Some time before; soldiers from Aram
decisions.reason: Readable shows that the raid happened before the story begins, which the Hebrew marks with the verb form, and names the raiders as soldiers.

records.source: וַתֹּ֨אמֶר֙ אֶל־גְּבִרְתָּ֔הּ אַחֲלֵ֣י אֲדֹנִ֔י לִפְנֵ֥י הַנָּבִ֖יא אֲשֶׁ֣ר בְּשֹׁמְר֑וֹן אָ֛ז יֶאֱסֹ֥ף אֹת֖וֹ מִצָּרַעְתּֽוֹ׃
records.gloss: And she said to her mistress, Would that my master [were] before the prophet who [is] in Samaria! Then he would gather him from his scale disease.
pieces: She said to her mistress, "If only my master could stand before the prophet in Samaria! Then he would free him from his skin disease."

L.3: And she said to her mistress, "If only my master [were] before the prophet who [is] in Samaria! Then he would gather him from his scale disease."

R.3: She said to her mistress, "I wish my master would go to see the prophet who lives in Samaria. He would heal him of his skin disease."

decisions.choice: gather him from his scale disease: free him from it, so that he can be received back among people
decisions.reason: The verb means "gather" or "take in". In Numbers 12:14-15 Miriam is "gathered in" to the camp after her skin disease; here the same verb is used of curing the disease, perhaps because healing let a person be taken back into the community. It is used this way again in verses 6, 7 and 11.

decisions.choice: the prophet in Samaria: Elisha
decisions.reason: Elisha had gone to Samaria, the capital of the northern kingdom, after Elijah was taken up (2:25), and he has a house there (verse 9). The girl knows of him from home.

decisions.choice: if only: a wish
decisions.reason: The word expresses a strong wish (Psalm 119:5). The girl speaks with confidence: if Naaman reaches the prophet, he will be healed.

decisions.choice: gather him from
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the Hebrew verb so that the reader can see the picture behind it; Balanced and Readable say "cure" and "heal".

records.source: וַיָּבֹ֕א וַיַּגֵּ֥ד לַאדֹנָ֖יו לֵאמֹ֑ר כָּזֹ֤את וְכָזֹאת֙ דִּבְּרָ֣ה הַֽנַּעֲרָ֔ה אֲשֶׁ֖ר מֵאֶ֥רֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵֽל׃
records.gloss: And he went and told his master, saying, Like this and like this spoke the girl who [is] from [the] land of Israel.
pieces: Naaman went in and told his master, "This is what the girl from the land of Israel said."

L.4: And he went in and told his master, saying, "Like this and like this the girl who [is] from the land of Israel has spoken."

R.4: Naaman went to the king and told him what the girl from Israel had said.

decisions.choice: he: Naaman; his master: the king of Aram
decisions.reason: The verse does not name either man, but the next verse shows that Naaman reported to the king.

decisions.choice: like this and like this: such and such, a summary of what was said
decisions.reason: The phrase stands for words already given, so the story does not repeat them (1 Kings 14:5).

decisions.choice: told him what the girl from Israel had said
decisions.reason: Readable gives the report as reported speech, since the words were given in verse 3, and names the master as the king.

records.source: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר מֶֽלֶךְ־אֲרָם֙ לֶךְ־בֹּ֔א וְאֶשְׁלְחָ֥ה סֵ֖פֶר אֶל־מֶ֣לֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל וַיֵּלֶךְ֩ וַיִּקַּ֨ח בְּיָד֜וֹ עֶ֣שֶׂר כִּכְּרֵי־כֶ֗סֶף וְשֵׁ֤שֶׁת אֲלָפִים֙ זָהָ֔ב וְעֶ֖שֶׂר חֲלִיפ֥וֹת בְּגָדִֽים׃
records.gloss: And said [the] king of Aram, Go, come, and I will send a letter to [the] king of Israel. And he went and took in his hand ten talents of silver and six thousand [of] gold and ten changes of garments.
pieces: The king of Aram said, "Go at once, and I will send a letter to the king of Israel." So Naaman went, taking with him {{units:about 750 pounds of silver|ten talents of silver}}, {{units:about 150 pounds of gold|6,000 shekels of gold}} and ten sets of fine clothes.

L.5: And the king of Aram said, "Go, come, and I will send a letter to the king of Israel." And he went and took in his hand ten talents of silver and 6,000 [shekels] of gold and ten changes of clothes.

R.5: The king of Aram said, "Go now. I will send a letter to the king of Israel." So Naaman set out. He took with him {{units:about 750 pounds of silver|ten talents of silver}}, {{units:about 150 pounds of gold|6,000 shekels of gold}} and ten sets of fine clothes.

decisions.choice: go, come: go at once
decisions.reason: Two verbs of motion together urge the hearer to set off without delay. The king approves the plan at once.

decisions.choice: a very large gift of silver and gold
decisions.reason: A talent was about 75 pounds of metal, so ten talents of silver was a great fortune. The unit of the gold is not stated; it is most likely the shekel, the usual weight for smaller sums. A great man going to ask for healing brought gifts to match his rank (1 Kings 14:3; 2 Kings 8:8-9).

decisions.choice: changes of garments: fine sets of clothes, given as gifts
decisions.reason: These were festive clothes that a person changed into for special occasions, and they were valued gifts (Genesis 45:22; Judges 14:12-13).

decisions.choice: took in his hand: took with him
decisions.reason: "In his hand" means in his keeping, not that he held it all himself (Genesis 43:12).

decisions.choice: about 750 pounds of silver; about 150 pounds of gold (6,000 shekels)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give modern weights, with the original units as the alternative: a talent is about 75 pounds and a shekel about 2/5 of an ounce. Literal keeps the units and brackets the shekel the Hebrew leaves unstated.

records.source: וַיָּבֵ֣א הַסֵּ֔פֶר אֶל־מֶ֥לֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל לֵאמֹ֑ר וְעַתָּ֗ה כְּב֨וֹא הַסֵּ֤פֶר הַזֶּה֙ אֵלֶ֔יךָ הִנֵּ֨ה שָׁלַ֤חְתִּי אֵלֶ֨יךָ֙ אֶת־נַעֲמָ֣ן עַבְדִּ֔י וַאֲסַפְתּ֖וֹ מִצָּרַעְתּֽוֹ׃
records.gloss: And he brought the letter to [the] king of Israel, saying, And now, when comes the letter this to you, behold, I have sent to you Naaman my servant, and you will gather him from his scale disease.
pieces: He brought the letter to the king of Israel. It said, "With this letter I am sending my servant Naaman to you, so that you may cure him of his skin disease."

L.6: And he brought the letter to the king of Israel, saying, "And now, when this letter comes to you, look, I have sent to you Naaman my servant, and you shall gather him from his scale disease."

R.6: Naaman took the letter to the king of Israel. It said, "I am sending my official Naaman to you with this letter. I want you to heal him of his skin disease."

decisions.choice: and now: the main business of the letter
decisions.reason: Letters began with greetings and then turned to their purpose with "and now" (10:2). Only the request is quoted here.

decisions.choice: my servant: Naaman as the king's high official
decisions.reason: A king's "servant" was any officer in his service, up to the highest (1 Kings 1:47). Naaman commands the army.

decisions.choice: you shall cure him: the king of Aram addresses the request to the king of Israel
decisions.reason: The girl spoke of a prophet, but the letter asks the king. A king would expect the healers and prophets of a kingdom to act at their king's command, and the request alarms the king of Israel (verse 7).

decisions.choice: my official
decisions.reason: Readable says "official" for a king's servant who holds high office, as these books do for the king's servants; Literal and Balanced keep "servant".

records.source: וַיְהִ֡י כִּקְרֹא֩ מֶֽלֶךְ־יִשְׂרָאֵ֨ל אֶת־הַסֵּ֜פֶר וַיִּקְרַ֣ע בְּגָדָ֗יו וַיֹּ֨אמֶר֙ הַאֱלֹהִ֥ים אָ֨נִי֙ לְהָמִ֣ית וּֽלְהַחֲי֔וֹת כִּֽי־זֶה֙ שֹׁלֵ֣חַ אֵלַ֔י לֶאֱסֹ֥ף אִ֖ישׁ מִצָּֽרַעְתּ֑וֹ כִּ֤י אַךְ־דְּעֽוּ־נָא֙ וּרְא֔וּ כִּֽי־מִתְאַנֶּ֥ה ה֖וּא לִֽי׃
records.gloss: And it was, when read [the] king of Israel the letter, and he tore his garments and said, [Am] God I, to kill and to make alive, that this [one] sends to me to gather a man from his scale disease? For only know, please, and see that seeking an occasion he [is] against me.
pieces: The king of Israel read the letter and at once tore his clothes. "Am I God," he said, "to put to death and to give life, that this man sends someone to me to be cured of his skin disease? Think about it and see: he is looking for a reason to quarrel with me."

L.7: And it happened, when the king of Israel read the letter, that he tore his clothes and said, "[Am] I God, to kill and to make alive, that this [man] sends to me to gather a man from his scale disease? But only know, please, and see that he is seeking an occasion against me."

R.7: The king of Israel read the letter and tore his clothes in alarm. He said, "Am I God? Can I kill people and bring them back to life? Why does this man send me someone and tell me to heal his skin disease? You can see that he is only looking for an excuse to fight me!"

decisions.choice: he tore his clothes: a sign of horror and distress
decisions.reason: Tearing one's clothes showed grief, alarm or despair (2 Samuel 13:19; 2 Kings 19:1). The king sees the letter as a threat he cannot meet.

decisions.choice: to kill and to make alive: power over life and death, which belongs to God alone
decisions.reason: The words recall Deuteronomy 32:39 and 1 Samuel 2:6, where God alone kills and makes alive. The king rightly knows that healing such a disease is beyond any human ruler, yet he does not think to turn to the prophet.

decisions.choice: seeking an occasion: looking for a pretext for war
decisions.reason: The verb means to seek an opportunity against someone; a related word is used in Judges 14:4. The king fears that when the cure fails, Aram will treat it as an insult and attack.

decisions.choice: the king of Israel: not named here
decisions.reason: The king is most likely Jehoram son of Ahab, who reigned in Samaria in Elisha's time (3:1). The story leaves him unnamed.

decisions.choice: in alarm; Why does this man ...
decisions.reason: Readable says what the torn clothes show and breaks the long question into three short questions.

records.source: וַיְהִ֞י כִּשְׁמֹ֣עַ׀אֱלִישָׁ֣ע אִישׁ־הָאֱלֹהִ֗ים כִּֽי־קָרַ֤ע מֶֽלֶךְ־יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ אֶת־בְּגָדָ֔יו וַיִּשְׁלַח֙ אֶל־הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ לֵאמֹ֔ר לָ֥מָּה קָרַ֖עְתָּ בְּגָדֶ֑יךָ יָבֹֽא־נָ֣א אֵלַ֔י וְיֵדַ֕ע כִּ֛י יֵ֥שׁ נָבִ֖יא בְּיִשְׂרָאֵֽל׃
records.gloss: And it was, when heard Elisha, [the] man of the God, that had torn [the] king of Israel his garments, and he sent to the king, saying, Why have you torn your garments? Let him come, please, to me, and he will know that there is a prophet in Israel.
pieces: Elisha the man of God learned that the king of Israel had torn his clothes, and he sent this word to the king: "Why have you torn your clothes? Let the man come to me, and he will find out that Israel has a prophet."

L.8: And it happened, when Elisha the man of God heard that the king of Israel had torn his clothes, that he sent to the king, saying, "Why have you torn your clothes? Let him come to me, please, and he will know that there is a prophet in Israel."

R.8: News reached Elisha the man of God that the king of Israel had torn his clothes. So he sent the king this message: "Why have you torn your clothes? Send the man to me. Then he will know that there is a prophet in Israel."

decisions.choice: the man of God: a title for a prophet
decisions.reason: Elisha is called "the man of God" through these chapters (4:7, 9; 5:14-15, 20). The title marks him as one who belongs to God and speaks for him.

decisions.choice: he will know that there is a prophet in Israel
decisions.reason: The king of Israel acts as though there were no help in Israel, as Ahaziah did when he sent to a foreign god (1:3, 6). Elisha answers that Yahweh's prophet is present. The healing will lead Naaman to know more: that there is no God except in Israel (verse 15).

decisions.choice: Let the man come (Balanced); Send the man (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name "the man" for "him", since the last man mentioned is the king.

records.source: וַיָּבֹ֥א נַעֲמָ֖ן בְּסוּסָ֣יו וּבְרִכְבּ֑וֹ וַיַּעֲמֹ֥ד פֶּֽתַח־הַבַּ֖יִת לֶאֱלִישָֽׁע׃
records.gloss: And came Naaman with his horses and with his chariot and stood [at the] entrance of the house of Elisha.
pieces: So Naaman came with his horses and his chariot and stopped at the door of Elisha's house.

L.9: And Naaman came with his horses and with his chariot and stood at the door of the house of Elisha.

R.9: So Naaman went with his horses and his chariot. He stopped at the door of Elisha's house.

decisions.choice: his horses
decisions.reason: The consonants written in the Hebrew text read "his horse"; the margin of the text tells readers to read "his horses", which is the reading followed here. The meaning hardly changes.

decisions.choice: his chariot: the chariot he rides, with its company
decisions.reason: The word can mean one chariot or a group of chariots. Naaman later gets down from his chariot (verse 21), and he travels with a large company (verse 15).

decisions.choice: he stood at the door: a great man arriving in state, waiting to be received
decisions.reason: Naaman comes with the full show of his rank and waits outside for the prophet to come out to him. What happens next offends him (verses 10-11).

records.source: וַיִּשְׁלַ֥ח אֵלָ֛יו אֱלִישָׁ֖ע מַלְאָ֣ךְ לֵאמֹ֑ר הָל֗וֹךְ וְרָחַצְתָּ֤ שֶֽׁבַע־פְּעָמִים֙ בַּיַּרְדֵּ֔ן וְיָשֹׁ֧ב בְּשָׂרְךָ֛ לְךָ֖ וּטְהָֽר׃
records.gloss: And sent to him Elisha a messenger, saying, Go and you will wash seven times in the Jordan, and will return your flesh to you, and be clean.
pieces: Elisha sent a messenger out to him to say, "Go and wash seven times in the Jordan. Your flesh will be restored, and you will be clean."

L.10: And Elisha sent a messenger to him, saying, "Go and wash seven times in the Jordan, and your flesh will return to you, and be clean."

R.10: Elisha sent a messenger out to tell him, "Go and wash yourself seven times in the Jordan River. Then your skin will be healed, and you will be clean."

decisions.choice: Elisha sent a messenger: he did not come out to meet Naaman
decisions.reason: A man of Naaman's rank expected the prophet to come out and receive him in person. Elisha gives the word through a messenger, so that the healing will rest on Yahweh's word alone and not on the prophet's presence, and Naaman takes offense (verse 11).

decisions.choice: seven times: a complete washing
decisions.reason: Seven marks completeness. The cleansing of a person healed of skin disease also uses seven: the priest sprinkles him seven times, and he waits seven days (Leviticus 14:7-9).

decisions.choice: your flesh will return to you, and be clean: your body will be restored and you will be clean
decisions.reason: "Flesh" is the body and its skin; it will come back to health. "Be clean" is the word for cleanness in the law (Leviticus 13:6, 13); though it has the form of a command, here it is a promise of what will follow.

decisions.choice: will be restored (Balanced); your skin will be healed (Readable); you will be clean
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what "will return" means, and turn the command "be clean" into the promise it is.

records.source: וַיִּקְצֹ֥ף נַעֲמָ֖ן וַיֵּלַ֑ךְ וַיֹּאמֶר֩ הִנֵּ֨ה אָמַ֜רְתִּי אֵלַ֣י׀יֵצֵ֣א יָצ֗וֹא וְעָמַד֙ וְקָרָא֙ בְּשֵׁם־יְהוָ֣ה אֱלֹהָ֔יו וְהֵנִ֥יף יָד֛וֹ אֶל־הַמָּק֖וֹם וְאָסַ֥ף הַמְּצֹרָֽע׃
records.gloss: And was angry Naaman and went and said, Behold, I said to myself, He will surely come out, and stand, and call on [the] name of Yahweh his God, and wave his hand over the place, and gather the scale-diseased.
pieces: But Naaman went away angry. He said, "I thought that he would surely come out to me, stand and call on the name of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} his God, wave his hand over the spot and cure me of the disease.

L.11: But Naaman was angry and went away and said, "Look, I said to myself, 'He will surely come out to me and stand and call on the name of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} his God, and wave his hand over the place, and gather the one with scale disease.'

R.11: But Naaman became angry and went away. He said, "I was sure that he would come out to meet me. I thought he would stand there and pray to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} his God. Then he would wave his hand over the sore place and heal me of the disease.

decisions.choice: he will surely come out: what Naaman had taken for granted
decisions.reason: The verb is doubled for emphasis. "I said to myself" means "I thought". Naaman had pictured a public healing worthy of his rank.

decisions.choice: wave his hand over the place: a healer's gesture over the diseased spot
decisions.reason: Naaman expected the prophet to pray aloud and move his hand over the sore part of the body. Instead he was told only to wash in a river.

decisions.choice: gather the one with scale disease: cure Naaman himself
decisions.reason: The last word means "the one with scale disease", that is, Naaman. Some take it as the diseased part of the skin; either way the sense is that the prophet would cure him.

decisions.choice: call on the name of Yahweh: pray to Yahweh, naming him
decisions.reason: To call on someone's name is to address that god in prayer (1 Kings 18:24).

decisions.choice: I thought that he would ... (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give Naaman's thought as reported speech instead of a quotation inside his speech, and say "cure me" for "the one with scale disease". Readable says "pray to" for "call on the name of". The speech continues into verse 12, so the quotation closes there.

records.source: הֲלֹ֡א טוֹב֩ אֲמָנָ֨ה וּפַרְפַּ֜ר נַהֲר֣וֹת דַּמֶּ֗שֶׂק מִכֹּל֙ מֵימֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל הֲלֹֽא־אֶרְחַ֥ץ בָּהֶ֖ם וְטָהָ֑רְתִּי וַיִּ֖פֶן וַיֵּ֥לֶךְ בְּחֵמָֽה׃
records.gloss: [Are] not better Abana and Pharpar, [the] rivers of Damascus, than all [the] waters of Israel? Could not I wash in them and be clean? And he turned and went in a rage.
pieces: Are not the rivers of Damascus, Abana and Pharpar, better than any of the waters of Israel? Could I not wash in them and be made clean?" Then he turned and went off in a fury.

L.12: [Are] not Abana and Pharpar, the rivers of Damascus, better than all the waters of Israel? Could I not wash in them and be clean?" And he turned and went away in a rage.

R.12: The Abana and the Pharpar are the rivers of Damascus. They are better than all the waters in Israel! Why could I not wash in them and become clean?" So he turned and left in a rage.

decisions.choice: Abana
decisions.reason: The consonants written in the Hebrew text spell "Abana"; the margin of the text tells readers to say "Amana", a name also found for a mountain in Song of Songs 4:8. Both forms name the same river, and the written form is kept here.

decisions.choice: Abana and Pharpar: rivers of Damascus
decisions.reason: Rivers fed by the snow of the mountains west of Damascus watered the city and its gardens. Their clear water seemed far better to Naaman than the muddy Jordan.

decisions.choice: two questions expecting the answer "yes"
decisions.reason: Naaman's questions mean: the rivers of Damascus are better, and he could have washed in them at home. He sees no reason why Israel's river should heal him.

decisions.choice: statement for the first question
decisions.reason: Readable turns the first question into a statement, since its answer is plain.

records.source: וַיִּגְּשׁ֣וּ עֲבָדָיו֮ וַיְדַבְּר֣וּ אֵלָיו֒ וַיֹּאמְר֗וּ אָבִי֙ דָּבָ֣ר גָּד֗וֹל הַנָּבִ֛יא דִּבֶּ֥ר אֵלֶ֖יךָ הֲל֣וֹא תַעֲשֶׂ֑ה וְאַ֛ף כִּֽי־אָמַ֥ר אֵלֶ֖יךָ רְחַ֥ץ וּטְהָֽר׃
records.gloss: And came near his servants and spoke to him and said, My father, [a] thing great [if] the prophet had spoken to you, would you not do [it]? And how much more when he has said to you, Wash and be clean.
pieces: His servants came up to him and said, "My father, had the prophet asked you to do something great, would you not have done it? How much more, then, should you obey when he tells you only, 'Wash and be clean'!"

L.13: And his servants came near and spoke to him and said, "My father, [if] the prophet had spoken a great thing to you, would you not have done [it]? How much more, then, when he has said to you, 'Wash and be clean'!"

R.13: Naaman's servants came to him and said, "Sir, if the prophet had told you to do something hard, you would have done it. So surely you can do it when he tells you only, 'Wash and be clean!'"

decisions.choice: my father: a respectful way to address a master
decisions.reason: The servants speak to Naaman as "father", a word of respect and affection for a superior (2 Kings 6:21; 13:14). The same letters could be read as a particle meaning "if", which gives "if the prophet had told you" with no address; the sense of the servants' argument is the same.

decisions.choice: how much more: an argument from the greater to the lesser
decisions.reason: If Naaman would have done something hard, he should all the more do something easy.

decisions.choice: his servants: the officers and attendants traveling with Naaman
decisions.reason: A commander's servants were men in his service, not owned slaves; they speak to him with respect and wisdom.

decisions.choice: Sir; something hard
decisions.reason: Readable says "Sir" for the respectful "my father", which sounds odd from servants in modern English, and "something hard" for "a great thing", that is, a great or difficult task.

records.source: וַיֵּ֗רֶד וַיִּטְבֹּ֤ל בַּיַּרְדֵּן֙ שֶׁ֣בַע פְּעָמִ֔ים כִּדְבַ֖ר אִ֣ישׁ הָאֱלֹהִ֑ים וַיָּ֣שָׁב בְּשָׂר֗וֹ כִּבְשַׂ֛ר נַ֥עַר קָטֹ֖ן וַיִּטְהָֽר׃
records.gloss: And he went down and dipped in the Jordan seven times, according to [the] word of the man of the God; and returned his flesh like [the] flesh of a boy young, and he was clean.
pieces: So he went down and dipped himself seven times in the Jordan, as the man of God had said. His flesh was restored and became like the flesh of a young boy, and he was clean.

L.14: And he went down and dipped himself in the Jordan seven times, according to the word of the man of God; and his flesh returned like the flesh of a young boy, and he was clean.

R.14: So Naaman went down to the Jordan River and dipped himself in it seven times, as the man of God had told him. His skin became healthy again, like the skin of a young boy. He was clean!

decisions.choice: dipped himself: went under the water
decisions.reason: The verb means to dip or plunge (Genesis 37:31; Leviticus 14:6). Naaman went fully into the river, seven times as he was told.

decisions.choice: a young boy: an echo of the young girl of verse 2
decisions.reason: The words for "young boy" match those used of the captive girl in verse 2. Through the word of a young girl, the great commander's flesh becomes like a young boy's.

decisions.choice: according to the word of the man of God ... and he was clean
decisions.reason: The healing comes exactly as the prophet said (verse 10). The writer stresses that it was Yahweh's word, spoken through Elisha, that cleansed him, not the river.

decisions.choice: his flesh was restored (Balanced); his skin became healthy again (Readable)
decisions.reason: As in verse 10, Balanced and Readable say what "his flesh returned" means. Readable speaks of the skin, where the disease showed.

records.source: וַיָּשָׁב֩ אֶל־אִ֨ישׁ הָאֱלֹהִ֜ים ה֣וּא וְכָֽל־מַחֲנֵ֗הוּ וַיָּבֹא֮ וַיַּעֲמֹ֣ד לְפָנָיו֒ וַיֹּ֗אמֶר הִנֵּה־נָ֤א יָדַ֨עְתִּי֙ כִּ֣י אֵ֤ין אֱלֹהִים֙ בְּכָל־הָאָ֔רֶץ כִּ֖י אִם־בְּיִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל וְעַתָּ֛ה קַח־נָ֥א בְרָכָ֖ה מֵאֵ֥ת עַבְדֶּֽךָ׃
records.gloss: And he returned to [the] man of the God, he and all his camp, and came and stood before him and said, Behold, please, I know that there is no God in all the earth except in Israel. And now take, please, a blessing from your servant.
pieces: Then he went back to the man of God with all his company. He came and stood before him and said, "Now I know that in all the earth there is no God except in Israel. So now, please accept a gift from your servant."

L.15: And he returned to the man of God, he and all his camp, and came and stood before him and said, "Look, now I know that there is no God in all the earth except in Israel. And now, please take a blessing from your servant."

R.15: Then Naaman went back to the man of God, along with all his people. He stood in front of Elisha and said, "Now I know that there is no God anywhere in the world except in Israel. Please accept a gift from me."

decisions.choice: no God in all the earth except in Israel: Yahweh, the God of Israel, is the only true God
decisions.reason: Naaman confesses what Elisha said he would learn (verse 8). The king of Israel had said "Am I God?" (verse 7); the foreign commander now knows who God is. The same confession is heard in Deuteronomy 4:35, 39 and 1 Kings 18:39.

decisions.choice: a blessing: a gift
decisions.reason: A gift given in thanks or good will can be called a "blessing" (Genesis 33:11; 1 Samuel 25:27). Naaman offers the wealth he brought (verse 5).

decisions.choice: your servant: a polite way of saying "me"
decisions.reason: The commander now speaks of himself as the prophet's servant, a courtesy that also shows his new humility (compare verse 9).

decisions.choice: his camp: his whole traveling company
decisions.reason: The word for a camp is used here of all the men, horses and chariots traveling with Naaman.

decisions.choice: me (Readable)
decisions.reason: Readable says "me" for the polite "your servant", as it does elsewhere in these books.

records.source: וַיֹּ֕אמֶר חַי־יְהוָ֛ה אֲשֶׁר־עָמַ֥דְתִּי לְפָנָ֖יו אִם־אֶקָּ֑ח וַיִּפְצַר־בּ֥וֹ לָקַ֖חַת וַיְמָאֵֽן׃
records.gloss: And he said, [As] lives Yahweh, whom I stand before him, if I will take. And he urged him to take, and he refused.
pieces: But Elisha said, "As surely as {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} lives, whom I serve, I will accept nothing." Naaman pressed him to take it, but he refused.

L.16: And he said, "[As] {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} lives, before whom I stand, I will not take [anything]." And he urged him to take [it], but he refused.

R.16: But Elisha said, "I serve {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. As surely as {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} lives, I will not take anything." Naaman kept urging him to take the gift, but Elisha refused.

decisions.choice: as Yahweh lives, before whom I stand: a solemn oath, and a claim to serve Yahweh
decisions.reason: Swearing by the life of Yahweh is the strongest oath. To "stand before" someone is to serve him, as Elijah used the same words (1 Kings 17:1; 18:15; 2 Kings 3:14).

decisions.choice: if I take: in an oath, "I will not take"
decisions.reason: In an oath, "if I do this" leaves a curse unspoken, so it means "I will not do it".

decisions.choice: Elisha refuses any gift
decisions.reason: The healing is Yahweh's free gift, not a service bought from a prophet. Elisha's refusal also keeps Naaman from thinking that he has paid for it. Gehazi's greed (verses 20-27) stands against this.

decisions.choice: whom I serve (Balanced); I serve the LORD (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what "before whom I stand" means, as in 1 Kings 17:1 and 18:15. Literal keeps the picture.

records.source: וַיֹּאמֶר֮ נַעֲמָן֒ וָלֹ֕א יֻתַּן־נָ֣א לְעַבְדְּךָ֔ מַשָּׂ֥א צֶֽמֶד־פְּרָדִ֖ים אֲדָמָ֑ה כִּ֡י לֽוֹא־יַעֲשֶׂה֩ ע֨וֹד עַבְדְּךָ֜ עֹלָ֤ה וָזֶ֨בַח֙ לֵאלֹהִ֣ים אֲחֵרִ֔ים כִּ֖י אִם־לַיהוָֽה׃
records.gloss: And said Naaman, And if not, let be given, please, to your servant [a] load of [a] pair of mules [of] earth; for not will offer again your servant burnt offering and sacrifice to gods other, except to Yahweh.
pieces: Then Naaman said, "If not, then please let your servant be given a load of earth, as much as a pair of mules can carry, because your servant will never again offer burnt offering or sacrifice to other gods, but only to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

L.17: And Naaman said, "If not, then please let there be given to your servant a load of earth [for] a pair of mules, for your servant will no longer offer burnt offering or sacrifice to other gods, but only to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

R.17: Then Naaman said, "If you will not take a gift, then please let me take home as much soil as two mules can carry. From now on I will not offer burnt offerings or sacrifices to any other gods. I will offer them only to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

decisions.choice: and if not: if you will not take a gift
decisions.reason: Naaman asks for something else since Elisha will not accept his gift. The words could also mean "if not, then at least"; the sense is the same.

decisions.choice: a load of earth from Israel: soil from Yahweh's land, to worship Yahweh on in Aram
decisions.reason: People in that world often thought of a god as bound to his own land; David speaks of being driven out to serve other gods when he is driven from Yahweh's land (1 Samuel 26:19). Naaman wants to worship Yahweh at home on soil taken from Yahweh's land. He most likely means to build an altar of earth (Exodus 20:24), but the text does not say so.

decisions.choice: no more offerings to other gods, but only to Yahweh
decisions.reason: Naaman turns from the gods of Aram to Yahweh alone. He uses the words for the burnt offering and the sacrifice as Israel's own law does (Exodus 20:24).

decisions.choice: your servant: a polite way of saying "I"
decisions.reason: As in verse 15.

decisions.choice: me, I (Readable); take home; If you will not take a gift
decisions.reason: Readable says "me" and "I" for the polite "your servant", and spells out what "if not" refers to and where the earth is going.

records.source: לַדָּבָ֣ר הַזֶּ֔ה יִסְלַ֥ח יְהוָ֖ה לְעַבְדֶּ֑ךָ בְּב֣וֹא אֲדֹנִ֣י בֵית־רִמּוֹן֩ לְהִשְׁתַּחֲוֺ֨ת שָׁ֜מָּה וְה֣וּא׀נִשְׁעָ֣ן עַל־יָדִ֗י וְהִֽשְׁתַּחֲוֵ֨יתִי֙ בֵּ֣ית רִמֹּ֔ן בְּהִשְׁתַּחֲוָיָ֨תִי֙ בֵּ֣ית רִמֹּ֔ן יִסְלַח־יְהוָ֥ה לְעַבְדְּךָ֖ בַּדָּבָ֥ר הַזֶּֽה׃
records.gloss: In the matter this may pardon Yahweh your servant: when goes my master [into the] house of Rimmon to bow down there, and he leans on my hand, and I bow down [in the] house of Rimmon, when I bow down [in the] house of Rimmon, may pardon Yahweh your servant in the matter this.
pieces: But in one matter may {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} pardon your servant: when my master goes into the temple of Rimmon to bow down there, he leans on my arm, and I too bow down in the temple of Rimmon. When I bow down in the temple of Rimmon, may {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} pardon your servant in this matter."

L.18: In this matter may {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} pardon your servant: when my master goes into the house of Rimmon to bow down there, and he leans on my hand, and I bow down [in] the house of Rimmon, when I bow down [in] the house of Rimmon, may {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} pardon your servant in this matter."

R.18: But there is one thing I ask {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} to forgive me for. When my master the king goes into the temple of Rimmon to worship, he leans on my arm, so I must bow down there too. When I bow in Rimmon's temple, may {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} forgive me for this."

decisions.choice: Rimmon: the chief god of Damascus
decisions.reason: Rimmon was the god worshiped in Damascus, probably the storm god Hadad under a title meaning "Thunderer". The name is found in the names of Aramean kings, such as Tabrimmon (1 Kings 15:18).

decisions.choice: Naaman asks in advance for pardon for bowing in Rimmon's temple when he must attend his king
alternatives: Naaman asks pardon for what he has done in the past
decisions.reason: Naaman has just vowed to worship Yahweh alone (verse 17). As the king's chief officer he will still have to go with him into Rimmon's temple and bow when the king bows. He does not call this worship of Rimmon; he names it as a thing needing pardon and asks Yahweh to forgive it. Elisha's answer, "Go in peace" (verse 19), does not discuss the request, and whether it grants it is not said.

decisions.choice: he leans on my hand: the king leans on Naaman's arm
decisions.reason: To lean on an officer's arm was the place of the king's closest attendant (7:2, 17). When the king bows, the officer bows with him.

decisions.choice: bow down: the act of worship, bowing to the ground
decisions.reason: The verb means to bow low, and it is the usual word for worship (Exodus 20:5). It is said three times here of Naaman and the king.

decisions.choice: your servant: a polite way of saying "me"
decisions.reason: As in verse 15.

decisions.choice: temple (Balanced, Readable) for "house"; arm for "hand"; my master the king; so I must
decisions.reason: The "house" of a god is his temple, and Balanced and Readable say so. Readable names the master as the king, says "me" for "your servant", and says what the Hebrew implies: Naaman's duty means he must bow with the king.

records.source: וַיֹּ֥אמֶר ל֖וֹ לֵ֣ךְ לְשָׁל֑וֹם וַיֵּ֥לֶךְ מֵאִתּ֖וֹ כִּבְרַת־אָֽרֶץ׃ס
records.gloss: And he said to him, Go in peace. And he went from him a stretch of land.
pieces: Elisha said to him, "Go in peace." So Naaman left him and went some distance.

L.19: And he said to him, "Go in peace." And he went from him a stretch of land.

R.19: Elisha told him, "Go in peace." So Naaman left, and he traveled a short way.

decisions.choice: go in peace: a farewell blessing
decisions.reason: The words send a person away with good will and wish him well (1 Samuel 1:17; 20:42). Elisha does not answer Naaman's request in so many words; the farewell leaves it with Yahweh.

decisions.choice: a stretch of land: some distance, length unknown
decisions.reason: The phrase is used for the distance still to go in Genesis 35:16 and 48:7. Its exact length is not known; here it was short enough for Gehazi to catch up on foot (verse 21).

decisions.choice: a short way
decisions.reason: Readable says "short" because Gehazi soon overtakes Naaman on foot.

records.source: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר גֵּיחֲזִ֗י נַעַר֮ אֱלִישָׁ֣ע אִישׁ־הָאֱלֹהִים֒ הִנֵּ֣ה׀חָשַׂ֣ךְ אֲדֹנִ֗י אֶֽת־נַעֲמָ֤ן הָֽאֲרַמִּי֙ הַזֶּ֔ה מִקַּ֥חַת מִיָּד֖וֹ אֵ֣ת אֲשֶׁר־הֵבִ֑יא חַי־יְהוָה֙ כִּֽי־אִם־רַ֣צְתִּי אַחֲרָ֔יו וְלָקַחְתִּ֥י מֵאִתּ֖וֹ מְאֽוּמָה׃
records.gloss: And said Gehazi, [the] young man of Elisha, [the] man of the God, Behold, has spared my master Naaman the Aramean this from taking from his hand what he brought. [As] lives Yahweh, surely I will run after him and take from him something.
pieces: Gehazi, the servant of Elisha the man of God, said to himself, "My master has let this Aramean Naaman off without taking any of the things he brought. As surely as {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} lives, I will chase after him and take something from him."

L.20: And Gehazi, the young man of Elisha the man of God, said, "Look, my master has spared Naaman this Aramean, not taking from his hand what he brought. [As] {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} lives, I will surely run after him and take something from him."

R.20: Gehazi, the servant of Elisha the man of God, thought, "My master let Naaman, this man from Aram, off too easily. He did not take any of the gifts Naaman brought. As surely as {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} lives, I will chase after him and take something from him."

decisions.choice: young man: servant, personal attendant
decisions.reason: The word means a young man, and often a servant or attendant (1 Kings 18:43). Gehazi has served Elisha in the story of the Shunammite woman (4:12, 25).

decisions.choice: said: said to himself
decisions.reason: No one is with Gehazi; "said" here means that he thought or decided.

decisions.choice: spared this Aramean: let him go without paying
decisions.reason: The verb means to hold back or spare. Gehazi thinks his master was too easy on a foreigner, and "this Aramean" carries his contempt for Naaman.

decisions.choice: as Yahweh lives: Gehazi swears the oath his master swore
decisions.reason: Elisha swore by Yahweh's life that he would take nothing (verse 16); Gehazi swears by the same name that he will take something. The writer sets the two oaths side by side.

decisions.choice: the servant (Balanced, Readable); said to himself (Balanced), thought (Readable); off too easily (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "servant" for "young man" and show that the words are Gehazi's thoughts. Readable says what "spared" means here and splits the sentence.

records.heading: Gehazi's greed

records.source: וַיִּרְדֹּ֥ף גֵּיחֲזִ֖י אַחֲרֵ֣י נַֽעֲמָ֑ן וַיִּרְאֶ֤ה נַֽעֲמָן֙ רָ֣ץ אַחֲרָ֔יו וַיִּפֹּ֞ל מֵעַ֧ל הַמֶּרְכָּבָ֛ה לִקְרָאת֖וֹ וַיֹּ֥אמֶר הֲשָׁלֽוֹם׃
records.gloss: And pursued Gehazi after Naaman, and saw Naaman [one] running after him, and he fell from on the chariot to meet him and said, [Is it] peace?
pieces: So Gehazi hurried after Naaman. When Naaman saw someone running after him, he got down from his chariot to meet him and asked, "Is everything all right?"

L.21: And Gehazi pursued after Naaman. And Naaman saw [one] running after him, and he got down from the chariot to meet him and said, "[Is it] peace?"

R.21: So Gehazi chased after Naaman. When Naaman saw a man running after him, he quickly got down from his chariot to meet him. He asked, "Is everything all right?"

decisions.choice: fell from the chariot: got down quickly
decisions.reason: The verb "fall" is used of getting down from a mount or chariot at once, as Rebekah does from her camel (Genesis 24:64). Naaman honors the prophet's servant by stepping down to meet him.

decisions.choice: is it peace?: is all well?
decisions.reason: The question asks whether all is well and whether the one coming brings good news (4:26; 9:17-22). Naaman wonders why the prophet's servant is running after him.

decisions.choice: got down (Literal)
decisions.reason: Literal says "got down" for "fell", since "fell from the chariot" would suggest an accident in English; meaning decision m1 gives the Hebrew picture.

records.source: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר׀שָׁל֗וֹם אֲדֹנִי֮ שְׁלָחַ֣נִי לֵאמֹר֒ הִנֵּ֣ה עַתָּ֡ה זֶ֠ה בָּ֣אוּ אֵלַ֧י שְׁנֵֽי־נְעָרִ֛ים מֵהַ֥ר אֶפְרַ֖יִם מִבְּנֵ֣י הַנְּבִיאִ֑ים תְּנָה־נָּ֤א לָהֶם֙ כִּכַּר־כֶּ֔סֶף וּשְׁתֵּ֖י חֲלִפ֥וֹת בְּגָדִֽים׃
records.gloss: And he said, Peace. My master has sent me, saying, Behold, now just this have come to me two young men from [the] hill country of Ephraim, from [the] sons of the prophets. Give, please, to them a talent of silver and two changes of garments.
pieces: He answered, "All is well. My master has sent me to say, 'Two young men of the company of prophets have just arrived from the hill country of Ephraim. Please give them {{units:about 75 pounds of silver|a talent of silver}} and two sets of clothes.'"

L.22: And he said, "Peace. My master has sent me, saying, 'Look, just now two young men have come to me from the hill country of Ephraim, from the sons of the prophets. Please give them a talent of silver and two changes of clothes.'"

R.22: Gehazi answered, "Everything is fine. My master sent me with this message: 'Two young men from the group of prophets have just arrived here from the hill country of Ephraim. Please give them {{units:about 75 pounds of silver|a talent of silver}} and two sets of clothes.'"

decisions.choice: my master has sent me: a lie
decisions.reason: Elisha has sent no one. Gehazi invents a message in his master's name to get the gifts the prophet refused (verses 16, 25-26).

decisions.choice: sons of the prophets: members of a group of prophets
decisions.reason: "Sons of" here means members of a group. These communities of prophets lived and learned around Elijah and Elisha (2:3-7; 4:1, 38).

decisions.choice: the hill country of Ephraim; a talent of silver
decisions.reason: The hill country of Ephraim is the central highlands of Israel, where Bethel lay (2:3). A talent, about 75 pounds of silver, is far less than Naaman brought (verse 5) but still a great sum, and it sounds like a plausible request for poor prophets.

decisions.choice: about 75 pounds of silver (a talent of silver)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the modern weight with the original unit as the alternative. "Company of prophets" and "group of prophets" follow the wording used for this phrase in these books.

records.source: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר נַעֲמָ֔ן הוֹאֵ֖ל קַ֣ח כִּכָּרָ֑יִם וַיִּפְרָץ־בּ֗וֹ וַיָּצַר֩ כִּכְּרַ֨יִם כֶּ֜סֶף בִּשְׁנֵ֣י חֲרִטִ֗ים וּשְׁתֵּי֙ חֲלִפ֣וֹת בְּגָדִ֔ים וַיִּתֵּן֙ אֶל־שְׁנֵ֣י נְעָרָ֔יו וַיִּשְׂא֖וּ לְפָנָֽיו׃
records.gloss: And said Naaman, Be pleased, take two talents. And he urged him, and he tied up two talents of silver in two bags and two changes of garments and gave [them] to two of his young men, and they carried [them] before him.
pieces: Naaman said, "Please, take {{units:about 150 pounds|two talents}}." He pressed Gehazi to take them, and tied up {{units:about 150 pounds of silver|two talents of silver}} in two bags, with two sets of clothes. He gave them to two of his servants, and they carried them ahead of Gehazi.

L.23: And Naaman said, "Be pleased to take two talents." And he urged him, and he tied up two talents of silver in two bags, and two changes of clothes, and gave [them] to two of his young men, and they carried [them] before him.

R.23: Naaman said, "Please take {{units:about 150 pounds|two talents}}." He kept urging Gehazi to take them. He tied up {{units:about 150 pounds of silver|two talents of silver}} in two bags, along with two sets of clothes. Then he gave them to two of his servants, and they carried them ahead of Gehazi.

decisions.choice: be pleased: a polite form of request
decisions.reason: The verb means to be willing or to agree; with a command it makes a courteous request (Judges 19:6).

decisions.choice: he urged him ... he tied ... before him: Naaman urges Gehazi, and the servants walk ahead of Gehazi
decisions.reason: The Hebrew uses "he" and "him" throughout. Naaman, glad to give, doubles the sum and sends two of his own men to carry it, one bag each.

decisions.choice: bags: purses or sacks that could be tied shut
decisions.reason: The word is used elsewhere only for a woman's handbag or purse (Isaiah 3:22). Here they are bags large enough for a talent of silver each.

decisions.choice: his young men: his servants
decisions.reason: As in verse 20, the word means attendants.

decisions.choice: about 150 pounds (two talents)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the modern weight, with the original unit as the alternative. They name Gehazi where the Hebrew says "him".

records.source: וַיָּבֹא֙ אֶל־הָעֹ֔פֶל וַיִּקַּ֥ח מִיָּדָ֖ם וַיִּפְקֹ֣ד בַּבָּ֑יִת וַיְשַׁלַּ֥ח אֶת־הָאֲנָשִׁ֖ים וַיֵּלֵֽכוּ׃
records.gloss: And he came to the hill, and took [them] from their hand and deposited [them] in [the] house; and he sent away the men, and they went.
pieces: When Gehazi came to the hill, he took the things from them and put them away in the house. Then he sent the men off, and they left.

L.24: And he came to the hill, and he took [them] from their hand and stored [them] in the house, and he sent the men away, and they went.

R.24: When Gehazi reached the hill, he took the bags and clothes from the servants and put them away inside the house. Then he sent the men away, and they left.

decisions.choice: the hill: a mound or raised, fortified place
decisions.reason: The word names a swelling or a hill, often the fortified height of a city (2 Chronicles 27:3; Micah 4:8). Here it is a place in Samaria near the house, whose location is now unknown.

decisions.choice: stored them in the house: Gehazi hid the goods before going to Elisha
decisions.reason: The verb means to put something in safekeeping. "The house" is probably the house where Elisha and Gehazi lived. Gehazi sends Naaman's men back at the hill, so they do not come with him to the prophet.

decisions.choice: Gehazi; the things, the bags and clothes
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name Gehazi and what he took, which the Hebrew leaves understood.

records.source: וְהוּא־בָא֙ וַיַּעֲמֹ֣ד אֶל־אֲדֹנָ֔יו וַיֹּ֤אמֶר אֵלָיו֙ אֱלִישָׁ֔ע מֵאַ֖יִן גֵּחֲזִ֑י וַיֹּ֕אמֶר לֹֽא־הָלַ֥ךְ עַבְדְּךָ֖ אָ֥נֶה וָאָֽנָה׃
records.gloss: And he went in and stood before his master. And said to him Elisha, From where, Gehazi? And he said, Not has gone your servant here or there.
pieces: Then he went in and stood before his master. Elisha asked him, "Where have you been, Gehazi?" He said, "Your servant has not gone anywhere."

L.25: And he went in and stood before his master. And Elisha said to him, "From where, Gehazi?" And he said, "Your servant has not gone here or there."

R.25: Then Gehazi went in and stood in front of his master. Elisha asked him, "Gehazi, where have you been?" Gehazi answered, "I have not been anywhere."

decisions.choice: from where
decisions.reason: The consonants written in the Hebrew text spell this word in a shorter form, and the margin of the text gives the usual spelling. Both mean "from where".

decisions.choice: here or there: anywhere
decisions.reason: The pair of words means "anywhere at all". Gehazi's answer is a second lie (verse 22).

decisions.choice: your servant: a polite way of saying "I"
decisions.reason: Gehazi uses the humble form of speech even as he lies to his master.

decisions.choice: Where have you been? (Balanced, Readable); I (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable complete Elisha's short question. Readable says "I" for "your servant".

records.source: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר אֵלָיו֙ לֹא־לִבִּ֣י הָלַ֔ךְ כַּאֲשֶׁ֧ר הָֽפַךְ־אִ֛ישׁ מֵעַ֥ל מֶרְכַּבְתּ֖וֹ לִקְרָאתֶ֑ךָ הַעֵ֞ת לָקַ֤חַת אֶת־הַכֶּ֨סֶף֙ וְלָקַ֣חַת בְּגָדִ֔ים וְזֵיתִ֤ים וּכְרָמִים֙ וְצֹ֣אן וּבָקָ֔ר וַעֲבָדִ֖ים וּשְׁפָחֽוֹת׃
records.gloss: And he said to him, Not my heart went when turned a man from on his chariot to meet you? [Is it] the time to take the silver and to take garments and olive groves and vineyards and sheep and cattle and male slaves and female slaves?
pieces: But Elisha said to him, "Was not my heart there with you when a man turned from his chariot to meet you? Is this a time for taking money and taking clothes, olive groves and vineyards, sheep and cattle, male slaves and female slaves?

L.26: And he said to him, "Did not my heart go [with you] when a man turned from his chariot to meet you? [Is it] the time to take the silver and to take clothes, and olive groves and vineyards, and sheep and cattle, and male slaves and female slaves?

R.26: But Elisha said to him, "Did you think I did not know? My spirit was with you when the man stepped down from his chariot to greet you. This is not the time to take money and clothes. It is not the time to take olive groves and vineyards, sheep and cattle, or slaves, both men and women.

decisions.choice: did not my heart go with you?: I was with you in spirit and saw what happened
alternatives: My heart did not depart [from you]
Was not my heart going [with you]?
decisions.reason: The Hebrew is very brief: "Not my heart went?" Read as a question, it means that Elisha was present in his inner self and knew all that Gehazi did, as prophets are given to see what is hidden (6:12). It can also be read as a statement, "My heart did not go away", meaning that Elisha was not unaware; the sense is close. The wording is hard and its exact force is uncertain.

decisions.choice: is it the time?: now is not the time
decisions.reason: The question expects "no". With Naaman newly turned to Yahweh, and with the healing given freely, this was no time to profit from it (verse 16).

decisions.choice: olive groves, vineyards, flocks, herds and slaves: what the silver could buy
decisions.reason: Elisha lists the property a man could acquire with the money: land, animals and servants. He sees what Gehazi meant to do with his gain. The list echoes the warning of what a king would take (1 Samuel 8:14-17).

decisions.choice: a man turned from his chariot: Naaman turned and got down
decisions.reason: The verb means to turn. Naaman turned from his chariot, that is, got down and turned to meet Gehazi (verse 21).

decisions.choice: male slaves and female slaves at every level
decisions.reason: The slaves are listed as property to be acquired with money, so "slave" is kept at every level, as the style of this translation does where people are owned or bought.

decisions.choice: Did you think I did not know?; statements for the second question
decisions.reason: Readable adds a short question that says what Elisha's words imply, and turns the rhetorical question into two statements. The added question goes beyond the Hebrew and rests on the reading in meaning decision m1.

records.source: וְצָרַ֤עַת נַֽעֲמָן֙ תִּֽדְבַּק־בְּךָ֔ וּֽבְזַרְעֲךָ לְעוֹלָ֑ם וַיֵּצֵ֥א מִלְּפָנָ֖יו מְצֹרָ֥ע כַּשָּֽׁלֶג׃ס
records.gloss: And [the] scale disease of Naaman will cling to you and to your offspring forever. And he went out from before him having scale disease, like snow.
pieces: So Naaman's skin disease will cling to you and to your descendants forever." And Gehazi went out from his presence with a serious skin disease, as white as snow.

L.27: And the scale disease of Naaman shall cling to you and to your offspring forever." And he went out from before him with scale disease, like snow.

R.27: So Naaman's skin disease will now cling to you and to your descendants forever!" When Gehazi left Elisha, he had the serious skin disease. His skin was as white as snow.

decisions.choice: Naaman's disease will cling to you: the punishment fits the sin
decisions.reason: Gehazi took what was Naaman's, and now he takes Naaman's disease. The disease "clings" as Naaman's silver had been carried to him. "To your offspring forever" makes it a curse on his line, as in 1 Samuel 2:31-33 and 2 Samuel 3:29.

decisions.choice: like snow: probably white, or flaking like snow
decisions.reason: The same comparison is used of Moses' hand and of Miriam (Exodus 4:6; Numbers 12:10). It most likely describes white patches of diseased skin; it may refer to flaking skin. The disease itself is the one named in verse 1.

decisions.choice: he went out from before him: Gehazi left Elisha's presence
decisions.reason: Gehazi is named again in 8:4-5, where he tells the king about Elisha. The story does not say how that meeting fits with his disease.

decisions.choice: as white as snow (Balanced, Readable); with a serious skin disease
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable make the likely meaning of "like snow" explicit, as meaning decision m2 explains; Literal keeps the bare comparison. They name Gehazi and Elisha for "he" and "him".
